planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container-grown trees in spring or fall in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Hoopsii blue spruce needs excellent air circulation and struggles with the heat and humidity of the Deep South.

directions: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container-grown trees in spring or fall in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Hoopsii blue spruce needs excellent air circulation and struggles with the heat and humidity of the Deep South. Dense, stiff, silvery-blue needles cover a strongly pyramidal tree considered one of the bluest of all blue spruce cultivars, holding its intense icy-blue color better through the seasons than the species or many other named selections. It is a classic specimen or windbreak tree for cold-winter climates with good air movement, but performs poorly and is prone to needle cast disease and spider mites in hot, humid summer regions such as the Gulf South, where it is not a reliable long-term choice. Water deeply during establishment and dry spells, avoid overhead irrigation that keeps needles wet, and give it full sun and room to reach its substantial mature size.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Bird's Nest spruce is extremely slow-growing and well suited to foundation plantings and rock gardens where a large conifer would be inappropriate.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Bird's Nest spruce is extremely slow-growing and well suited to foundation plantings and rock gardens where a large conifer would be inappropriate. Dense, dark green needles cover a wide, flat-topped, mounding shrub with a distinctive central depression that gives the plant its common name, resembling a nest sunk into the top of the mound as the outer branches grow slightly taller than the congested center. One of the most popular dwarf Norway spruce cultivars, it grows only two to three inches per year, remaining a manageable, tidy specimen for foundation plantings, rock gardens, and mixed conifer beds for decades without pruning. It tolerates a range of soils and light conditions better than many dwarf conifers and needs only occasional watering during establishment and drought.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Blue Rug juniper tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil once established and rots in wet, poorly drained ground.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Blue Rug juniper tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil once established and rots in wet, poorly drained ground. Trailing, ground-hugging branches are densely clothed in intensely silvery-blue, needle-like foliage that lies nearly flat against the soil, spreading widely to form a dense, weed-suppressing mat rarely more than a few inches tall, one of the lowest and bluest of all groundcover junipers. Its low, spreading habit and rich blue color make it an excellent choice for cascading over a retaining wall, covering a dry sunny bank, or filling in between larger shrubs in a xeriscape planting, requiring no mowing or shearing to maintain its form. Water regularly during the first year to establish, then rely mainly on natural rainfall, and avoid overhead watering that keeps the dense foliage wet, which encourages fungal disease.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; dwarf Japanese garden juniper tolerates drought and poor soil once established and rots in wet, poorly drained ground.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; dwarf Japanese garden juniper tolerates drought and poor soil once established and rots in wet, poorly drained ground. Dense, soft-textured, blue-green needle foliage covers stiffly horizontal branches that layer over one another as the plant spreads, forming a low, textured, wave-like mound popular both as a durable groundcover and as classic material for outdoor bonsai and rock garden specimens. Its tight, compact branching and slightly mounded (rather than flat) habit compared to other groundcover junipers gives it more three-dimensional texture, useful for softening the edge of a rock garden, retaining wall, or foundation planting. Water regularly during the first year, then rely mainly on natural rainfall, and shear lightly if a more formal, tighter mound is wanted.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Mops mugo pine is extremely slow-growing and needs excellent drainage, tolerating drought and poor soil once established.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Mops mugo pine is extremely slow-growing and needs excellent drainage, tolerating drought and poor soil once established. Dense, dark green needles are held on tightly congested, irregularly rounded branches that grow just an inch or two per year, forming a naturally globe-shaped, tousled mound reminiscent of a mop head, one of the most popular true-dwarf mugo pine selections for foundation plantings and rock gardens. Its slow growth rate means it holds its neat, rounded form for decades with essentially no pruning required, making it an exceptionally low-maintenance evergreen accent for a small garden or entryway planting. Water during establishment and prolonged drought, and avoid heavy, poorly drained soils that can lead to root rot.
